questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman attended for a preoperative assessment 1 week before a scheduled tonsillectomy. She had a history of anxiety and mitral valve prolapse. She had a reported allergy to penicillin with transient rash and no other symptoms. She asked whether she needed antibiotic prophylaxis for endocarditis.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: She does not require prophylaxis because she does not have a high-risk cardiac condition
She does not require prophylaxis because she is not undergoing a high-risk procedure
She requires a preoperative echocardiogram to inform the decision
She should receive prophylaxis with amoxicillin
She should receive prophylaxis with clindamycin

questions.explanation: She does not require prophylaxis because she does not have a high-risk cardiac condition. High-risk cardiac conditions include prosthetic valves, previous endocarditis, congenital heart disease with unrepaired cyanotic defects, repaired defects with prosthetic materials in the first 6 months postrepair, repaired congenital defects with residual defects next to a prosthetic material, and cardiac transplant recipients with valvulopathy of the transplanted heart. MVP is not a high-risk condition, so she does not require antibiotic prophylaxis. If she were a candidate for prophylaxis and had a reliable history of penicillin allergy, clindamycin, azithromycin, or clarithromycin would be reasonable alternatives. A tonsillectomy is a high-risk procedure which involves incision of the respiratory mucosa. If she had one of the high-risk cardiac conditions mentioned above, then in the United States she would be a candidate for prophylaxis for tonsillectomy. In the UK, NICE guidance currently does not advise routine antibiotic prophylaxis against endocarditis, even in patients with cardiac conditions that are at higher risk of developing infective endocarditis. This is because the clinical effectiveness of antibiotic prophylaxis is not proven, it is not cost-effective, and there may be more deaths due to anaphylaxis than are prevented. An echocardiogram is not indicated.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q14

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman sought medical advice regarding long-term antibiotic prophylaxis. She was taking benzathine penicillin G every 3 weeks. She had been diagnosed and treated for rheumatic fever when she was 15 years old after developing subcutaneous nodules, polyarthritis, and carditis. Her last echocardiogram showed no residual valvular disease.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Continue until at least age 40, and possibly lifelong
No indication for any further prophylaxis
Stop prophylaxis but give a rescue box of antibiotics for GAS pharyngitis

questions.explanation: Continue prophylaxis until age 25 All patients with rheumatic fever should receive secondary prophylaxis independent of the presence or absence of carditis and/or residual heart disease; these will only affect the DURATION of prophylaxis. The patient has known RF with carditis but no residual cardiac manifestations. In this case the recommendation is for patients to continue prophylaxis for at least 10 years from diagnosis or until age 21, whichever is longer. Since she was diagnosed at age 15, she should receive prophylaxis until age 25 which is longer than age 21. Short term duration of prophylaxis is only recommended for patients who have RF with no evidence of cardiac involvement. The recommendation to treat until age 40 or lifelong is for patients with RF with carditis and residual valvular disease, which this patient does not have. She has no indication to switch to oral antibiotics, although this could be considered. The success rates of oral prophylaxis at preventing relapse are lower than parenteral prophylaxis even with 100% adherence. Episodes of GAS pharyngitis in the patient or in household contacts should be treated promptly but not at the expense of continuing prophylaxis.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q15

questions.model_answer:
a) Per the 2014 AHA guideline, the non-congenital high-risk cardiac conditions are: (1) prosthetic cardiac valve (mechanical, bioprosthetic, or prosthetic material used for valve repair); (2) previous infective endocarditis; (3) cardiac transplant recipient with valve regurgitation due to a structurally abnormal valve.
b) None. Prophylaxis for gastrointestinal (or genitourinary) procedures specifically to prevent IE is no longer recommended, even in high-risk patients such as unrepaired cyanotic CHD; antibiotic prophylaxis is limited to high-risk dental procedures.

questions.model_answer: a) MRSA PVE: Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h plus Rifampin 300 mg PO/IV q8h, both for >=6 weeks, plus Gentamicin 3 mg/kg/day in 2-3 divided doses for the first 2 weeks. b) (1) Previous infective endocarditis; (2) prosthetic cardiac valve (or prosthetic material used for valve repair); (3) cardiac transplant recipient who develops valvulopathy. c) No antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended for colonoscopy/GI endoscopy; prophylaxis solely to prevent endocarditis is not indicated for GI procedures even in high-risk cardiac patients (give it only to treat an established GI infection).
questions.beyond_mandell: Parts b and c follow the 2007 AHA/IDSA prevention of infective endocarditis guideline (Wilson et al.); this chapter does not list the specific prophylaxis indications.

cohort_answer.text: Prosthetic valve IE: 6 weeks total therapy - Vancomycin + Rifampin x6 weeks, plus gentamicin for first 2 weeks. a) Previous infective endocarditis; transplant with valvulopathy; prosthetic valve (congenital cardiac ones: cyanotic heart disease within 6 months of repair, or repaired with ongoing non-epithelialized areas). b) No prophylaxis (respiratory tract biopsy IS an indication for prophylaxis; debridement of infected skin/soft tissue).

B) 2 congenital heart conditions for which ppx is indicated?
C) 2 non-congenital heart conditions for which ppx is indicated?
D) 2 procedures for which ppx is indicated?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Congestive heart failure from valvular dysfunction (the strongest indication). (2) Uncontrolled/persistent infection (perivalvular or myocardial abscess, new heart block, persistent bacteremia/fever despite appropriate therapy). (3) Ineffective antimicrobial therapy (e.g., fungal IE, highly resistant organisms). (4) Prevention of embolism: recurrent systemic emboli or a large (>1 cm, especially anterior mitral leaflet) persistent vegetation. b) (1) Unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease; (2) repaired CHD with prosthetic material within the first 6 months, or repaired CHD with a residual defect at/adjacent to prosthetic material. c) (1) Prosthetic cardiac valve or prosthetic valve-repair material; (2) previous infective endocarditis (also cardiac transplant recipients with valvulopathy). d) (1) Dental procedures manipulating gingival tissue, the periapical region, or perforating oral mucosa; (2) procedures incising respiratory-tract mucosa (e.g., tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy, bronchoscopy with biopsy of respiratory mucosa).
questions.beyond_mandell: Prophylaxis indications (parts b-d) rest on the AHA 2007 (reaffirmed) IE prevention guideline, not the chapter slice.

cohort_answer.text:
Acute CHF and valvular insufficiency; Aortic root abscess; New heart block; Valvular dehiscence; Size > 1cm (particularly for anterior leaflet mitral valve); Persistent embolization >1 during first 2 weeks of tx; Persistent bacteremia/fever despite 5-7 days on appropriate tx
Unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease ("The 5T's"): Tricuspid atresia; Tetralogy of fallot; Total anomalous pulmonary venous return; Truncus arteriosus; Transposition of the great arteries
Previous IE; Prosthetic cardiac valves; Post cardiac transplant with cardiac valvulopathy
All dental procedures that involve manipulation of gingival tissue; Tonsillectomy, adenoidectomy; Bronchoscopy with bx of respiratory mucosa

questions.question: A man with a prosthetic mitral valve. What is the endocarditis prophylaxis (if needed) — give drug, dose, mode of administration, and frequency — for each of the following procedures.
questions.question_raw: Prosthetic valve ppx. Man with prosthetic mitral valve. What is the endocarditis ppx (if needed). Give name of drug, dose, mode of administration, frequency.

parts.text: Bronchoscopy
Hernia repair
Cystoscopy

parts_raw.text: Bronchoscopy
Hernia repair
Cystoscopy

questions.model_answer:
a) Bronchoscopy: none indicated. Common diagnostic procedures including bronchoscopy may occasionally induce bacteremia but carry minimal IE risk, so prophylaxis to prevent IE is no longer recommended.
b) Hernia repair: none indicated (a clean, non-infected surgical procedure; GI/GU/orthopedic prophylaxis specifically to prevent IE is no longer recommended).
c) Cystoscopy: none indicated. Prophylaxis for genitourinary procedures specifically to prevent IE is no longer recommended.
questions.beyond_mandell: AHA adds an exception not detailed in this chapter: for highest-risk patients, a respiratory-tract procedure involving incision/biopsy of respiratory mucosa (e.g., rigid bronchoscopy with biopsy) warrants amoxicillin 2 g PO 30-60 min prior.

cohort_answer.text:
Bronchoscopy – not recommended unless biopsy of respiratory mucosa done: Amoxicillin 2g (50mg/kg/dose for kids) PO 30-60min before procedure
Hernia repair – none indicated
Cystoscopy – none indicated

questions.model_answer:
a) No — gastrointestinal endoscopy/sclerotherapy prophylaxis specifically to prevent IE is no longer recommended, even with prior IE.
b) Yes — prosthetic valve is a high-risk condition and a dental procedure with gingival manipulation is an indication; give amoxicillin 2 g PO 30-60 min before (clindamycin 600 mg if penicillin-allergic).
c) No — bicuspid aortic valve is not a high-risk condition, and genitourinary procedure prophylaxis is no longer recommended.
d) No — mitral stenosis is not a listed high-risk condition, and bronchoscopy prophylaxis to prevent IE is no longer recommended.
